title: White-tailed Deer
summary: Deer connect Long Island woodland ecology with Shinnecock material knowledge and the continuing art of making regalia.
content:
Woodlands and their edges

The white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) belongs to Long Island’s living landscape. Deer move between woodland shelter and places where they can browse. At Flax Pond, the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation identifies deer among the native mammals of the surrounding habitat.[1]

Hide, sinew, bone, and antler

The Shinnecock Environmental Department’s 2014 catalogue records knowledge shared by Shinnecock Elders. Its deer entry describes hides used for clothing, blankets, door coverings, and moccasins; sinew for sewing; and bone and antler for tools, jewelry, and other worked objects. These materials required knowledge and patient skill to prepare and shape.[2]

Deer hide in regalia

Regalia can carry the history of a particular person and community. The Long Island Museum documents regalia made around 1995 for Setalcott Chief Blue Medicine, Theodore “Ted” Green (1927–2007). Its materials include deer hide, glass beads, shell, sinew, and thread. This named example connects deer to contemporary Native artistry on Long Island.[3]

Look closely

When viewing regalia, look for the maker, wearer, community, and materials in its caption. How does knowing those details change what you see?

The moving animal is an illustration of habitat and movement, not a live sighting or a route to wildlife.

References

  1. NYSDEC, Flax Pond Tidal Wetland Area
  2. Shinnecock Environmental Department, Natural Resources Identified by Shinnecock Elders (2014), animal entries. Project research archive.

why_this_matters: A deer on the landscape connects ecology with skilled work: clothing, sewing, toolmaking, and the personal histories carried by regalia. Learning those connections helps us recognize Native knowledge in both everyday materials and museum collections.
